newsitem.title: UK: DOLLAR STEADIES, FOCUS ON MARK/YEN AND STERLING.
newsitem.headline: DOLLAR STEADIES, FOCUS ON MARK/YEN AND STERLING.

text.p: The dollar steadied below Wednesday's peaks against other major currencies as traders focused on the mark's slide to two-year lows against the yen and sterling's likely reaction to any interest rate move later on Thursday.
Concern about the potential for trade tensions between the U.S. and Japan was kept alive by remarks made on Wednesday by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.

This fuelled demand for yen, causing the dollar to pare gains from the 12-week highs it had set against the Japanese currency on Wednesday. It also drove the mark down to 62.75 yen, the weakest it has been since July 1995.
The pound was also a talking point, with traders expecting the Bank of England's monetary policy committee to announce at 1100 GMT if it has decided to raise rates from 6.75 percent.
"The yen strengthened quite a bit overnight on the trade issue and there were quite a few mark/yen plays going on," said Craig Justham, deputy fx manager at Creditanstalt Bankverein.
"Sterling has also recovered a bit from yesterday's lows as people are waiting for the rate news but it shouldn't rise too far even if they do hike rates."
Dollar/mark was at 1.8839/44 at 0750 GMT from 1.8788/92 late on Thursday and yesterday's near-eight-year high of 1.8913.
The U.S. currency was at 118.59/69 yen from 119.01/11 late in Europe on Thursday. Mark/yen was at 63.00/03 from 63.44/46 late yesterday.

The dollar has climbed 8.1 percent in the last two months against the yen, but so far fallen shy of topping 120 yen amid concern this will elicit a barrage of verbal intervention from Japanese, and possibly U.S., officials.
"The markets know there is some sort of political barrier at this level and expect comments from Japan if it tries to creep up here," said Stewart Newnham, economist at First Chicago in London.
Japan is expected by traders to protest against such dollar gains to pre-empt U.S. complaints about any widening in its bilateral trade deficit with Japan.

Comments made yesterday by U.S. trade official Barshefsky reinforced these expectations. She said Japan should not rely too much on exports to promote growth and that she was disappointed by the recent drop in U.S. automotive sales to Japan.
First Chicago's Newnham expects trading in the yen to take its cue now from the June Japanese current account data which will be released on Friday.

Trading in dollar/mark, meantime, is expected to be dominated by speculation about whether the Bundesbank will engineer higher money market rates by switching to a variable rate tender to set its securities repurchase rate.
Analysts expect the German central bank to take such a step if the mark extends its slide much beyond 1.90 marks.
"The warning lights are flashing amber but they are not on red alert," said Newnham at First Chicago. "But a move up to 1.95 (marks) and a bit beyond could be the cue for a move."
Dollar bulls are, however, betting German economic recovery is not yet robust enough to withstand a significant rate rise.
They are therefore betting that the dollar's one-pfennig slide from yesterday's peaks against the mark is no more than a temporary setback on the way up to a test of 1.90.

"The market has a 1.90 target in mind and if it has a target it will go there," said James McKay, economist at PaineWebber. "The dollar has pushed up to these highs on relatively little news so it needs little new incentive to get there."
-- Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom
